items.title: Mock 2 — Summarize Group Discussion Q1 (Choosing next semester's courses)
items.transcript:
Narration: three students are discussing which course to take next semester.

Speaker1: Have you guys checked out the course list for next semester? I skimmed through it yesterday and chose the design-survey course that involves advanced research skills. To be honest, I don't really like it, but I think it is useful for my studies. For me, high grades are not everything. Sometimes, we need to think beyond academic performance. As long as a course brings personal benefits and supports our future careers, that is good enough.

Speaker2: I think it is right to choose a useful course. I'm also okay with doing research, and I would like to choose business. However, it requires statistics, and I'm quite poor at data processing. I'm a little worried that I might find it difficult to keep up with the coursework. But I suppose improving my skills in this area would be beneficial in the long run.

Speaker3: Well, you both choose useful courses, but I have a different opinion. I prefer courses that I am genuinely interested in, without considering whether they would be useful for future career development. After all, we spend a lot of time studying, so I think we should enjoy the learning process rather than just focus on our future jobs.

Speaker1: I see your point, but courses you like are not necessarily easy to pass. Sometimes, even interesting subjects involve difficult assignments and exams. Passing is the top priority, especially because we need enough credits to graduate.

Speaker3: That's true, but I don't think courses are difficult only if you like them. I believe that as long as I am interested in a subject, I can focus on it and pass it. That's why I have chosen Spanish, although it does not help me much, as my major is business and finance. I just want to learn something different.

Speaker2: Actually, Spanish is useful for you, since your major involves foreign trade and you may work with Spaniards in the future. It could give you more job opportunities. In fact, I think languages are useful for any major because communication skills are important in almost every industry.

Speaker1: Yes, I agree. Learning a language would also be beneficial for me. It could help us communicate with people from different countries and understand other cultures. To sum up, although our methods are different, everyone's goal is to graduate and obtain a degree. Everyone has their own choice. Just enjoy what you choose!

items.title: Mock 2 — Summarize Group Discussion Q2 (Campus part-time jobs)
items.transcript:
Narration: Three students are debating the pros and cons of campus part-time jobs, gathered at a corner table in the student lounge, the air filled with the faint smell of coffee and the rustle of textbook pages.

Speaker1: I think working part-time on campus is a total waste of energy. Last month I took a job at the library desk, and between shelving books and scanning IDs, I barely had any mental capacity left for my coursework. I ended up dozing off during my morning lectures twice last week.

Speaker2: Actually, I find my part-time job at the academic office really helpful. It forces me to manage my time better. I used to procrastinate all afternoon, but now I block out my shifts and study hours in advance. Plus, I'm earning my own spending money—it feels good not to have to ask my parents for every little thing.

Speaker3: But the workload is no joke. I tried working at the campus café last semester and it drained me completely. Some days I'd finish my shift at 8 pm, and then still have to write a lab report due at midnight. I got so stressed I had to quit after a month. It's not just about time—it's the mental toll.

Speaker1: Exactly! And let's be honest—most of these jobs don't even relate to our future careers. I'd rather join a student club or work on a project that actually builds my resume. Stuffing envelopes or swiping cards isn't going to help me get into grad school.

Speaker2: I see what you mean, but you're overlooking the soft skills. I've learned to talk to supervisors, handle complaints, and show up on time—that's real-world experience. And it's not always about the job itself; it's about showing you can balance responsibilities.

Speaker3: I guess, but I still think it depends on your schedule. If you're taking 18 credits like I am this semester, adding a job is just unrealistic. The stress isn't sustainable. Maybe if the university limited work hours to under 10 per week... but even then, I'd rather use that time to review or sleep.

Speaker1: Same. I'd prefer a work-study program that's more flexible and aligned with my major. Maybe assisting a professor with research instead of stacking books. That way I'm earning and learning at the same time. Otherwise, it just feels like trading precious study hours for tasks that don't contribute to my long-term goals.

Speaker2: That's a fair point. I wouldn't say no to a more relevant job either. But still, even a simple job teaches discipline. And let's be real—not all of us can get those research assistant roles. Sometimes starting with a basic job can actually open doors to those better opportunities later on.

Speaker3: Well, if I'm going to work, I'd want it to mean something beyond the paycheck. Otherwise, I'd rather focus on my grades. There has to be a balance. Burnout is real, and no amount of money is worth compromising both my health and academic performance.
